h1: Hiring seasonal and casual staff for brewpub peak months
title: Hiring seasonal staff for brewpub peaks | Craft Beer School
desc: How an Indian brewpub can plan, hire, train and manage seasonal and casual staff for peak months without hurting service, beer quality or compliance.
teaser: The busiest weeks of the year are the worst time to discover you are three servers short.
standfirst: Brewpub demand in India swings with weather, festivals and sport. Permanent staff alone either leave you short in the peaks or overstaffed in the troughs. Here is how to plan casual and seasonal hiring so the busy months go well.
sections: Know your peaks before you hire

Start with your own POS data: covers by week for the last year, plus the nights when service broke down. Most brewpubs see peaks around the festive season, the year-end and New Year, big cricket tournaments and, in many cities, the hot months when beer sells fastest. The monsoon is often quieter. Our guide to planning a brewpub year around Indian seasons maps the usual pattern.

From covers, work out staff hours needed per shift by role: floor, bar, kitchen, host and cleaning. Compare that with your permanent team's hours. The gap is your seasonal hiring plan, week by week.

Not every job can be handed to someone who started on Monday. Hosts, runners, glass collectors, cleaning and some kitchen prep roles can be learned quickly. Bar staff who pour beer need more training, especially on a draught system with long lines and several beers at different carbonation levels. Brewing roles should stay with your permanent team. A casual worker should never be put in charge of a fermenter or a CIP cycle.

A good pattern is to move experienced permanent staff into the harder roles during peaks and fill the simpler roles with casual hires.

• Hospitality and hotel management students looking for paid experience.
  • Former staff who left on good terms and may want a few months of work.
  • Referrals from your current team, which often bring reliable people.
  • Staffing agencies for volume, with clear agreements on who is the employer and who pays statutory dues.

Start recruiting six to eight weeks before the peak. By the time the festive rush starts, the good people are already working elsewhere.
Train for the beer, not just the floor

Guests in a brewpub ask about the beer. A casual server who cannot explain the difference between the wheat beer and the IPA hurts sales and the brand. Give every new hire a short beer briefing: each beer on tap, how it tastes, what it pairs with, alcohol strength and which beers are stronger than they look.

Bar staff need practical training on pouring: the right glass, the right head and what to do when a keg starts fobbing. Two hours with the head brewer before the first shift pays for itself in wasted beer saved.

Every person serving alcohol must know your state's minimum legal drinking age and your rules for checking ID, refusing service to intoxicated guests and helping guests get home safely. Make it a written briefing, signed on the first day. Busy nights are when mistakes happen. New staff are the ones most likely to give in to a pushy table.

Check also that each staff member meets the minimum age your state sets for working in licensed premises.

Peak nights are not peak all night. A brewpub may be calm at 7 PM and overwhelmed from 9 to 11. Stagger casual shifts to match: a runner who starts at 8:30 is more useful than one who starts at 6 and is tired by the rush. Build the roster from hourly covers in your POS, not from habit.

Pair every new casual hire with an experienced team member for their first few shifts. Put the roster up at least a week ahead, so people can plan and you find out early who cannot make it.

Casual does not mean informal. Give each hire a written letter with role, pay, hours and duration. Pay at least the minimum wage for your state and category. Check when provident fund, state insurance and other registrations apply to your headcount. Food handlers usually need medical fitness records under food safety rules. If you use an agency, confirm in writing that it meets these obligations, because liability can come back to you.

Rules vary by state and change, so ask your accountant or an HR consultant to check your setup before the peak. Our guide to brewery staffing covers the permanent team side.

Run a short review once the rush is over: which nights were understaffed, which hires were strong and which training gaps showed. Keep contact details of the good people and offer them first refusal next season. A pool of returning casual staff who already know your beers is worth more than any agency.

Planning labour against demand is one of the clearest ways a brewpub protects its margin. It is a skill that sits squarely in running the business rather than brewing the beer.
faqs: When should a brewpub start hiring for peak season?
Six to eight weeks before the peak, so you can train people properly and still find good candidates.
Which roles can casual staff handle?
Hosts, runners, glass collectors, cleaning and some kitchen prep. Bar work needs more training. Brewing should stay with permanent staff.
Do casual staff need training in responsible service?
Yes. Everyone serving alcohol must know the legal drinking age, ID checks and when to refuse service, from their first shift.
Do labour laws apply to seasonal staff?
Yes. Minimum wages and statutory registrations can apply depending on your state and headcount. Check with an accountant or HR consultant.
